message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"dbf20dd6560a1745c61e7a02bd19050010b5396824aad3f19aa2adf8c775fa64","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-co-class-std:lineage:69","source_registry_sha256":"bdc8d5a61f622fc6c91da0be8478dfb02615c007374129c91888edf82eb1b746","units":[{"unit_id":"sec03-u01","module_id":"sec03-m01","objective_ids":["sec03-u01"],"title":{"text":"Marijuana and driving","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Marijuana harms both thinking and physical driving skills, so impaired driving raises the risk of death or injury.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01"]},{"text":"Because THC levels do not track impairment, cases lean heavily on how the driver actually behaved.","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-R02"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"A driver uses marijuana, then drifts across a lane and struggles with field tests; the blood test later shows three nanograms of THC per milliliter.","fact_ids":["sec03-F05","sec03-R02"]},"reasoning":{"text":"The level is below the DUI inference, but DWAI has no THC inference level and behavior plus blood results can prove impairment.","fact_ids":["sec03-F05","sec03-R01"]},"result":{"text":"The driver can still be convicted, because behavior evidence matters most in marijuana cases.","fact_ids":["sec03-F05","sec03-R02"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a driver below five nanograms of THC cannot be charged with an impaired-driving offense.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01"]},"correction":{"text":"The five-nanogram inference applies to DUI only; DWAI has no THC level, and behavior with blood results can prove it.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-F05"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"THC numbers mislead; behavior tells.","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-R02"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A test shows five nanograms of THC per milliliter of blood. Which impaired-driving charge can the law infer from that level?","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-R01"]},"answer":{"text":"DUI.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04"]},"rationale":{"text":"The five-nanogram inference applies to DUI only; DWAI has no THC inference level.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Marijuana behind the wheel","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"How it impairs.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]},{"text":"Why levels mislead.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]},{"text":"What the law infers.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Marijuana is legal for adults in Colorado, but driving while impaired by it is not. This lesson explains what marijuana does to a driver, why its effects vary so much from person to person, and why a THC test result is a poor measure of impairment. Then we cover the one number the law does attach to THC, a permissible inference for DUI, and the important point that DWAI has no such number at all. That combination is why most marijuana cases are built on how a driver behaved, with blood results as support rather than as the whole story.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Thinking and physical skills","fact_ids":["sec03-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Judging and planning.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01"]},{"text":"Coordination, reaction time, tracking.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01"]},{"text":"Higher risk of death or injury.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Marijuana affects two families of driving skills. The first is thinking skills, such as judging distances and planning your moves. The second is physical skills, such as coordination, reaction time and tracking, which is the ability to follow a lane or a moving vehicle smoothly. Because it hits both families at once, driving while impaired by marijuana raises the risk of death or injury. A driver may feel calm and careful, yet still misjudge a gap or react late to a car braking ahead. Feeling relaxed is not the same as being able to drive safely.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Why effects vary","fact_ids":["sec03-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Dose and time since use.","fact_ids":["sec03-F02"]},{"text":"The individual.","fact_ids":["sec03-F02"]},{"text":"How it was consumed.","fact_ids":["sec03-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"How impaired marijuana makes you depends on several things: the dose, the time since use, the individual, and the way it was consumed. An edible can affect a person differently, and on a different schedule, than smoking. Two friends using the same amount can end up with very different levels of impairment. This variability is one reason drivers misjudge their own condition. Waiting a short while may not be enough, and a person who felt fine last time may not feel fine this time. The safest choice is not to drive after using marijuana at all.","fact_ids":["sec03-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"THC levels mislead","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"THC level does not track impairment.","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-R02"]},{"text":"Unlike BAC for alcohol.","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-R02"]},{"text":"Behavior evidence matters most.","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a key difference from alcohol. For alcohol, BAC roughly reflects impairment. For marijuana, the amount of THC measured in blood, breath or saliva does not track how impaired a person actually is. Someone with a low reading can be badly impaired, and someone with a higher reading may be less affected at that moment. That is why behavior evidence matters so much in marijuana cases. How the driver drove, what the officer saw during the stop, and how the driver did on field sobriety tests often carry more weight than the test number alone.","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"The inference is DUI only","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Five nanograms per milliliter of blood.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]},{"text":"Permissible inference of DUI.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]},{"text":"No THC level for DWAI.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Colorado law allows a permissible inference of DUI when a driver has five nanograms of THC per milliliter of blood. Learners often stretch that number into a safe line, assuming anyone below five nanograms is in the clear. Not so. The inference applies to DUI only, and there is no THC inference level for DWAI at all. Most marijuana-impaired drivers are convicted on their behavior together with their blood THC results. So a driver at three nanograms who weaves and fails field tests can still face DWAI. Five nanograms is an inference for one charge, not a permission slip.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Which charge fits","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-R01","sec03-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Five nanograms of THC.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-R01","sec03-F05"]},{"text":"Which charge does it support?","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-R01","sec03-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a driver's blood test shows five nanograms of THC per milliliter of blood. Which impaired-driving charge does Colorado's permissible inference support, and what about the other charge? Decide before reading on. The inference supports DUI. DWAI has no THC inference level, so a DWAI case would rest on the driver's behavior together with the blood results. And remember the bigger lesson: THC levels do not track impairment the way BAC roughly does for alcohol, so a lower number never proves a driver was safe to drive.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-R01","sec03-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Marijuana recap","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Harms thinking and physical skills.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]},{"text":"THC level does not track impairment.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]},{"text":"Inference for DUI only.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us review. Marijuana affects thinking skills like judging and planning and physical skills like coordination, reaction time and tracking, so impaired driving raises the risk of death or injury. How impaired it makes you depends on dose, time since use, the individual and how it was consumed. Unlike alcohol, measured THC does not track impairment. Colorado allows a permissible inference of DUI at five nanograms of THC per milliliter of blood, but DWAI has no THC level, and most cases rest on behavior together with blood results. Next, we look at mixing drugs and the penalties that follow.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F03","sec03-F04","sec03-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec03-u02","module_id":"sec03-m02","objective_ids":["sec03-u02"],"title":{"text":"Other drugs and penalties","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F07","sec03-F08"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Mixing drugs can strengthen their effects, which makes polydrug impairment especially dangerous.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06"]},{"text":"Officers prove impairment from any cause, so no drug choice or low test amount makes impaired driving safe from conviction.","fact_ids":["sec03-F08"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"A driver takes a prescription pain killer, drinks one beer, and drives home feeling only slightly off.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Using two or more drugs at once, including alcohol, is polydrug impairment, and the mix can strengthen the effects.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06"]},"result":{"text":"The driver is more impaired than either substance alone would suggest and can be convicted based on observed impairment.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F08"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking an impaired-driving charge can be bargained down to a lesser offense.","fact_ids":["sec03-F15"]},"correction":{"text":"Colorado does not allow plea bargaining an alcohol or drug driving offense down; never driving after using is the only sure protection.","fact_ids":["sec03-F15","sec03-F14"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Mix multiplies; no bargaining down.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F15"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A driver mixes a prescription sedative with alcohol. What is this called?","fact_ids":["sec03-F06"]},"answer":{"text":"Polydrug impairment.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06"]},"rationale":{"text":"Using two or more drugs at once, in any mix including alcohol, is polydrug impairment, and the mix can strengthen effects.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Beyond a single drug","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-F15"]},"lines":[{"text":"Mixing drugs.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-F15"]},{"text":"Illegal drugs.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-F15"]},{"text":"Severe penalties.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-F15"]}],"narration":{"text":"So far you have learned about alcohol and marijuana one at a time. This lesson widens the view. Many impaired drivers have more than one substance in their system, and the combination can be worse than either alone. You will also learn how illegal drugs affect drivers, how officers recognize impairment no matter which drug caused it, and why the penalties for alcohol or drug driving offenses are severe, with no option to bargain the charge down. The message by the end is direct: the only sure protection is never driving after using alcohol or drugs.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-F15"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Polydrug impairment","fact_ids":["sec03-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Two or more drugs at once.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06"]},{"text":"Any mix, including alcohol.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06"]},{"text":"Effects can strengthen.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Polydrug impairment means using two or more drugs at once, in any mix of alcohol, marijuana, prescription, over-the-counter or other drugs. The mix can strengthen the effects, so one drink plus a sedative can impair a driver far more than either would alone. That is why a driver who feels only slightly off after combining substances can be dangerously impaired. Polydrug use does not require any illegal drug at all. A cold remedy and a glass of wine count as a mix. Whenever two substances are in play, assume the effects are stronger than you expect.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Illegal drugs","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"LSD, methamphetamine, heroin.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F08"]},{"text":"Harm reflexes, judgment, alertness.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F08"]},{"text":"False confidence or drowsiness.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Illegal drugs such as LSD, methamphetamine and heroin harm reflexes, judgment and alertness. Depending on the drug, they can create false confidence, leading a driver to take risks they would never normally take, or leave a driver too drowsy to react. Both outcomes are dangerous in different ways. A driver who feels invincible may speed and weave, while a drowsy driver may fail to notice a stopped car. Officers are trained to recognize and testify about impaired driving from any cause, and drivers are convicted regardless of which drug was involved or how much was found in blood or saliva.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"No bargaining it down","fact_ids":["sec03-F15","sec03-F14"]},"lines":[{"text":"No plea bargaining down.","fact_ids":["sec03-F15","sec03-F14"]},{"text":"Jail, fines, license loss.","fact_ids":["sec03-F15","sec03-F14"]},{"text":"Never drive after using.","fact_ids":["sec03-F15","sec03-F14"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Some people assume they can negotiate an impaired-driving charge down to something minor. Colorado does not allow plea bargaining an alcohol or drug driving offense down. Penalties for these offenses are severe and can include jail, fines and loss of driving privileges. So the only sure protection is never driving after using alcohol or drugs. When a practice question offers an answer that lets a driver escape the charge through a deal, or treats a first offense as a simple ticket, that answer misses the rule. Planning a sober ride is the real protection.","fact_ids":["sec03-F15","sec03-F14"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Name the mix","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"A sedative plus alcohol.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F08"]},{"text":"What is it called?","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: before driving home, a person takes a prescription sedative and then has a glass of wine at dinner. What is this kind of impairment called, and why does it matter? Think it through before reading on. It is polydrug impairment, which means using two or more drugs at once in any mix, including alcohol. The mix can strengthen the effects, so the driver may be far more impaired than either substance alone would suggest. And because officers can prove impairment from any cause, a legal prescription offers no protection from a charge.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Other drugs recap","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-F14","sec03-F15"]},"lines":[{"text":"Mixes strengthen effects.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-F14","sec03-F15"]},{"text":"Any drug can lead to conviction.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-F14","sec03-F15"]},{"text":"Severe penalties, no plea deals.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-F14","sec03-F15"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us wrap up. Polydrug impairment means using two or more drugs at once, in any mix, and the mix can strengthen the effects. Illegal drugs such as LSD, methamphetamine and heroin harm reflexes, judgment and alertness and can bring false confidence or drowsiness. Officers recognize impairment from any cause, and drivers are convicted regardless of which drug or how much. Penalties include jail, fines and loss of driving privileges, and Colorado does not allow plea bargaining these offenses down. Never drive after using alcohol or drugs. Next, we look at chemical tests and refusal.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-F14","sec03-F15"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec03-u03","module_id":"sec03-m03","objective_ids":["sec03-u03"],"title":{"text":"Express consent and refusal","fact_ids":["sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-R07"]},"why_how":[{"text":"By driving in Colorado you have already agreed to a chemical test, so refusing carries its own heavy penalty.","fact_ids":["sec03-F09","sec03-F11"]},{"text":"An ignition interlock prevents a driver from starting the car with elevated alcohol, which protects the public after a refusal.","fact_ids":["sec03-F12"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"A driver stopped for weaving refuses every chemical test and later also receives a suspension from the same incident.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-F13"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Refusal brings a one-year revocation and two years of interlock, and the other suspension is added after the refusal revocation ends.","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F13"]},"result":{"text":"The driver serves the refusal revocation first, then the additional suspension, with an interlock required for two years.","fact_ids":["sec03-R04","sec03-R03"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking other suspensions from the same incident run at the same time as the refusal revocation.","fact_ids":["sec03-R04"]},"correction":{"text":"Other penalties from the same incident are added onto the end of the refusal revocation, served consecutively.","fact_ids":["sec03-R04","sec03-F13"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Refuse: one year out, two years blowing.","fact_ids":["sec03-R03"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A driver refuses a chemical test. How long is the revocation, and how long is the interlock requirement?","fact_ids":["sec03-F11","sec03-R03"]},"answer":{"text":"A one-year revocation and a two-year ignition interlock requirement.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11"]},"rationale":{"text":"Refusal brings two different periods, one year and two years, and other same-incident penalties are added afterward.","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-R04"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Chemical tests and consent","fact_ids":["sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"What you agreed to.","fact_ids":["sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-F13"]},{"text":"What refusal costs.","fact_ids":["sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-F13"]},{"text":"How penalties stack.","fact_ids":["sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers what happens when an officer asks you for a chemical test. Colorado's Express Consent Law means the agreement already happened when you chose to drive. You will learn which kinds of samples can be required, the penalties for refusing or not cooperating, how an ignition interlock works, and how other penalties from the same incident are timed. Refusal is sometimes imagined as a clever way to avoid a charge. As you will see, the handbook treats it as its own serious violation, with two separate time periods attached and more added on afterward.","fact_ids":["sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The Express Consent Law","fact_ids":["sec03-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Driving means consent.","fact_ids":["sec03-F09"]},{"text":"A chemical test for alcohol or drugs.","fact_ids":["sec03-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Under the Express Consent Law, driving in Colorado means you have agreed to a chemical test for alcohol or drugs. You do not sign anything at the roadside to give this consent; it comes with the privilege of driving here. So when an officer suspects impaired driving and asks for a test, the question is not whether you agree, because you already have. The question is whether you will cooperate. Understanding this changes how you see refusal. Refusing is not declining a favor. It is breaking an agreement you made by getting behind the wheel on a Colorado road.","fact_ids":["sec03-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Four kinds of samples","fact_ids":["sec03-F10","sec03-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Blood, breath, saliva or urine.","fact_ids":["sec03-F10","sec03-R07"]},{"text":"Required when impairment is suspected.","fact_ids":["sec03-F10","sec03-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"When an officer suspects impaired driving, you can be required to give a blood, breath, saliva or urine sample for testing. People often picture only the breath test, but express consent covers all four. That matters for drug cases especially, since some drugs are better detected in blood, saliva or urine than in breath. So an answer that says express consent applies only to breath tests is wrong. The test type depends on the situation and on what the officer suspects. Whatever sample is requested, the same consent covers it, and the same refusal penalties apply if you do not cooperate.","fact_ids":["sec03-F10","sec03-R07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Refusal penalties","fact_ids":["sec03-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"One-year license revocation.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11"]},{"text":"Two years of ignition interlock.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11"]},{"text":"On any vehicle you drive.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"Refusing or failing to cooperate with the chemical test leads to a one-year license revocation plus a two-year requirement to use an ignition interlock on any vehicle you drive. Failing to cooperate counts the same as an outright refusal, so stalling or giving an incomplete sample is not a way around it. The interlock requirement applies to any vehicle you drive, not only your own car. These penalties come from the refusal itself, before any court decides whether you were impaired. That is why refusal is never a shortcut: it carries its own revocation even if no impaired-driving conviction follows.","fact_ids":["sec03-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"How an interlock works","fact_ids":["sec03-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Breath sample before starting.","fact_ids":["sec03-F12"]},{"text":"Repeat samples while driving.","fact_ids":["sec03-F12"]},{"text":"Will not start with elevated alcohol.","fact_ids":["sec03-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"An ignition interlock is a device connected to the vehicle. It requires a breath sample before the engine starts and repeat samples while you are driving. If it detects elevated alcohol, the vehicle will not start. The repeat samples matter: they stop a driver from having someone else blow into the device and then drinking after starting. During the two-year interlock requirement that follows a refusal, every vehicle you drive needs one. The device turns the rule into something the car itself enforces, which is why the handbook describes it in such practical, step-by-step terms.","fact_ids":["sec03-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s6","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"One year, two years","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Revocation: one year.","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F11"]},{"text":"Interlock: two years.","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F11"]},{"text":"Do not swap them.","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the first trap. Refusing a chemical test brings two different time periods: one year of revocation and two years of ignition interlock use. Questions love to swap them, offering two years of revocation and one year of interlock. Hold them in order: first you lose the license for one year, then the interlock requirement lasts two years. A useful check is that the interlock period is the longer one, because it is meant to follow you after you are allowed to drive again. If an answer makes the revocation longer than the interlock period, it has the two numbers reversed.","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Count the periods","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F11","sec03-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"A refused test.","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F11","sec03-R04"]},{"text":"How long is the revocation?","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F11","sec03-R04"]},{"text":"How long is the interlock?","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F11","sec03-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a driver stopped on suspicion of impaired driving refuses to give any sample. How long is the license revocation, and how long must the driver use an ignition interlock? Work it out before reading on. The revocation lasts one year, and the interlock requirement lasts two years on any vehicle the driver drives. If the same incident also brings another suspension, that suspension is added after the refusal revocation ends rather than running alongside it. And remember, by driving in Colorado, the driver had already agreed to the test.","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F11","sec03-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Express consent recap","fact_ids":["sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-F12","sec03-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Driving means consent.","fact_ids":["sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-F12","sec03-F13"]},{"text":"Blood, breath, saliva or urine.","fact_ids":["sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-F12","sec03-F13"]},{"text":"One year out, two years interlock.","fact_ids":["sec03-F09","sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-F12","sec03-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us review.
